Kabuki. A form of classical Japanese theater that emerged in the early seventeenth century and became the defining popular performance art of the Edo period. Characterized by stylized acting, elaborate costumes, spectacular staging, and predominantly male performers playing all roles including female characters, kabuki developed from street performance into a highly refined art form. It served as a mirror of urban merchant culture and a vehicle for both celebrating and critiquing social norms, making it essential to understanding Japanese aesthetics, literature, and society.

Kabuki originated in Kyoto around 1603 as an improvisational form performed by women. Later, after government morality crackdowns, it was restricted to male performers only. The form developed an elaborate system of acting styles, makeup called onnagata or female impersonation, and gesture that conveyed meaning to audiences who knew the conventions. Kabuki became the primary venue for performing plays by Chikamatsu Monzaemon and other dramatists, whose works explored love, duty, and tragic sacrifice. The theater featured elaborate stagecraft—trap doors, rotating platforms, and dynamic visual spectacle that pushed the technical innovation of the time to its limits. Throughout the Edo period, kabuki flourished as entertainment for merchants and townspeople in urban centers like Edo, which is now Tokyo, as well as Osaka and Kyoto. The tradition remains vital in modern Japan, with classical plays performed in styles unchanged for centuries. Bunraku, the puppet theater tradition, competed and cross-pollinated artistically with kabuki during the Edo period. Together, these performance traditions embodied Japan's urban culture and aesthetic values, and their influence shaped Japanese literature and theater for centuries to come.
